PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
CON
No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR
YES on Proposition 39—
Californians for Voter ID
Info@voteridca.org (mailto:Info@voteridca.org)
www.VoterIDCA.org (https://www.voteridca.org/)
AGAINST
No on Prop. 39—Californians
for Voting Rights

PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Got the official title/summary and analysis. Main provisions of Proposition 39:

1. Prohibits mail voting unless the voter specifies a government-issued ID number when registering to vote
2. If the last 4 digits of the specified government-issued ID number on the mail ballot envelope don't match the number registered, the ballot is invalidated (e.g., if the voter registered with a Social Security number but puts in a driver's license number on the envelope, that ballot is invalid)
3. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting a government-issued ID
4. Requires elections officials to report annually the percentage of voters in each county whose citizenship has been verified
5. Requires "best efforts" to verify the citizenship of registered voters
6. Creates a free state-issued voter ID card
7. Requires the State Auditor to conduct audits in odd-numbered years
8. Implementation requires legislative action (the legislature must specify which IDs are eligible, etc.)
9. Cost: tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars annually

Also, as an important point: "The legislature must pass additional legislation to implement this measure. The legislature must clarify several details not defined in the measure, such as which forms of ID can be used and what procedures count as 'best efforts' to verify citizenship status."

Next, let's grab the arguments and rebuttals, and do some web research on the following:
- Background: who proposed this (Transparency Foundation), and which IDs qualify
- Research on voter ID laws and voter suppression/turnout effects (e.g., studies on strict voter ID laws like the Texas 2013 law, which reduced Black turnout by about 6% / reduced African American voting participation)
- California-specific context: California is an all-mail-vote state (VBM), about 80% vote by mail, so the last-4-digits requirement on envelopes could produce a lot of invalid ballots
- Existing ID verification in California: at registration, you're already asked to provide a driver's license, state ID, or the last 4 digits of your SSN; if not provided, ID is required at first-time voting
- The noncitizen voting issue — California's existing process
- Comparison: other states that have ID laws
- Whether there are safeguards (provisional ballots, cure procedures, etc.)

Let's get the arguments and rebuttals, and search the web.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID

Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.
Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot.
In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.

Got the official title/summary and analysis. Main provisions of Proposition 39:

1. Prohibits mail voting unless the voter specifies a government-issued ID number when registering to vote
2. If the last 4 digits of the specified government-issued ID number on the mail ballot envelope don't match the number registered, the ballot is invalidated (e.g., if the voter registered with a Social Security number but puts in a driver's license number on the envelope, that ballot is invalid)
3. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting a government-issued ID
4. Requires elections officials to report annually the percentage of voters in each county whose citizenship has been verified
5. Requires "best efforts" to verify the citizenship of registered voters
6. Creates a free state-issued voter ID card
7. Requires the State Auditor to conduct audits in odd-numbered years
8. Implementation requires legislative action (the legislature must specify which IDs are eligible, etc.)
9. Cost: tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars annually

Also, as an important point: "The legislature must pass additional legislation to implement this measure. The legislature must clarify several details not defined in the measure, such as which forms of ID can be used and what procedures count as 'best efforts' to verify citizenship status."

Next, let's grab the arguments and rebuttals, and do some web research on the following:
- Background: who proposed this (Transparency Foundation), and which IDs qualify
- Research on voter ID laws and voter suppression/turnout effects (e.g., studies on strict voter ID laws like the Texas 2013 law, which reduced Black turnout by about 6% / reduced African American voting participation)
- California-specific context: California is an all-mail-vote state (VBM), about 80% vote by mail, so the last-4-digits requirement on envelopes could produce a lot of invalid ballots
- Existing ID verification in California: at registration, you're already asked to provide a driver's license, state ID, or the last 4 digits of your SSN; if not provided, ID is required at first-time voting
- The noncitizen voting issue — California's existing process
- Comparison: other states that have ID laws
- Whether there are safeguards (provisional ballots, cure procedures, etc.)

Let's get the arguments and rebuttals, and search the web.

39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. Don’t believe the lies. Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.
PROP. 39 IS FUNDED BY MAGA RIGHTWING BILLIONAIRES. Follow the money. MAGA billionaires have spent millions spreading election lies. Republican operatives have pushed this voter suppression agenda for years. They want Trump to have unlimited power so they get more tax breaks for the rich while cutting funding to healthcare and schools for the rest of us.
California election officials already verify voters. Prop. 39 just ADDS EXTRA HURDLES for citizens. THE FACTS DON’T LIE. When Texas tried this, they threw out 12 times more mail ballots than California.
Prop. 39 creates new threats of identity theft. No citizen should have to choose between their privacy and their right to vote.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found that Prop. 39 could COST HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS EACH YEAR—read it for yourself. MAGA extremists want to use your taxpayer dollars to buy Trump an expensive gift: blocking eligible voters and giving the Big Lie a win in California. We won’t fall for it.
PROP. 39 TRIES TO DISTRACT US from how Trump and his billionaire friends have failed Americans. Hospitals are closing. Fire victims are still waiting for help. Groceries and housing costs are more expensive than ever. Now they want to use Prop. 39 to control our elections and avoid accountability.
NO KINGS. NO LIES. NO PROP. 39.
Alex Padilla , U.S. Senator for California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39
VOTE NO. Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.
STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. Alright, I've got a solid grasp of the official materials. Next, let me dig into external research on the following:

1. Research on voter ID laws and turnout/suppression (e.g., the University of Chicago study on the 2013 Texas photo ID law: African American turnout dropped by about 6 percentage points; other studies showing that strict photo ID laws suppress minority turnout; versus studies showing no effect)
2. California's signature mismatch rejection rates (over 100,000 ballots rejected in 2024? Actually, the 2022 midterm: about 62,000 provisional/suspense ballots; the 2024 figure is what's being claimed). The "cure" process for signature issues.
3. The claim about Texas rejecting "12x the number of mail-in ballots" — Texas's mail-in ballot rejection rate was much higher than California's.
4. The non-citizen voting problem: how big is it? Research suggests that the scale of non-citizen voting is very small (the 2020 estimate was around 226,000 out of 161 million, with high uncertainty; the 2022 study estimated around 158,000–190,000, mostly accidental).
5. Which IDs are acceptable — the measure doesn't define it, and that's up to the legislature. Key uncertainty.
6. Legal challenges — e.g., the Democracy Docket court ruling on the title/summary.
7. California is 80%+ vote-by-mail (VBM). Adding a 4-digit requirement to the envelope = risk of ballot rejection if a single digit is wrong. Are there cure procedures? The Mercury News interview says "assuming eligible voters receive notice and the opportunity to correct errors" — but what does the actual measure say? Let me check the text of the measure for details on rejected ballots and provisional ballots.

Also, the key question is "is it better to vote yes or no?" — I need to make a judgment. Let me think through the arguments:

Arguments in favor of YES:
- Low-cost voter fraud is essentially nonexistent, but ID requirements increase trust in elections (public trust is a real problem post-2020).
- Most Americans support voter ID (polls show majority support; in California, the LA Times editorial? Let me check the editorial).
- Free voter ID cards for those who don't have one.
- The measure includes good governance elements: citizenship verification, audits, clean-up of the voter rolls.
- Bipartisan support among the general public (not politicians).

Arguments in favor of NO:
- Empirical research shows that strict voter ID laws have little to no effect on preventing fraud (fraud is rare), but they can suppress turnout, particularly among minorities, the elderly, low-income voters, and people of color. The Texas 2013 study (Franklin et al., University of Chicago / the Brennan Center?) — actually the famous study is "Voter ID Laws and Turnout" — the 2013 Texas law study by Mitchell Franklin et al. found that the 2013 Texas photo ID law reduced Black turnout by about 6 percentage points in 2014.
- In California, over 80% of voters vote by mail. Requiring 4 digits to be written on the envelope creates a new rejection/error pathway. One digit wrong → ballot invalidated. This is an "accuracy" risk that could be significant in a VBM state. California already does signature verification + cure.
- Cost: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year.
- Privacy/security concerns about writing SSN digits on the envelope.
- The measure is vague: which IDs qualify is up to the legislature — this is a significant weakness; it could lead to litigation and inconsistent implementation across counties.
- Non-citizen voting is a tiny problem (estimated at a small fraction of a percent of votes), and the existing process already requires citizenship certification under penalty of perjury.
- The ACLU, LWVCA, and Common Cause are opposed; Senator Padilla is also opposing; Newsom and Pelosi are also opposing.
- The "best efforts" citizenship verification could lead to erroneous purges of citizens (a real documented problem: states purging people through data matching mistakes, e.g., the 2011 Harvard study on purges in North Carolina, Florida).

This is a big deal: the measure's core mechanisms depend on future legislation, so there's a risk of uncertainty/fragmentation.

2. Data on the scale of non-citizen voting.

4. What the text of the measure says about rejected/provisional ballots (is there a cure procedure?).
5. Opinions of the editorial boards (e.g., NYT, WSJ, LA Times editorials on Prop 39).
6. Which IDs qualify per the measure or the proponents.

1. Research on voter ID laws and turnout/suppression (e.g., the University of Chicago study on the 2013 Texas photo ID law: African American turnout dropped by about 6 percentage points; other studies showing that strict photo ID laws suppress minority turnout; versus studies showing no effect)
2. California's signature mismatch rejection rates (over 100,000 ballots rejected in 2024? Actually, the 2022 midterm: about 62,000 provisional/suspense ballots; the 2024 figure is what's being claimed). The "cure" process for signature issues.
3. The claim about Texas rejecting "12x the number of mail-in ballots" — Texas's mail-in ballot rejection rate was much higher than California's.
4. The non-citizen voting problem: how big is it? Research suggests that the scale of non-citizen voting is very small (the 2020 estimate was around 226,000 out of 161 million, with high uncertainty; the 2022 study estimated around 158,000–190,000, mostly accidental).
5. Which IDs are acceptable — the measure doesn't define it, and that's up to the legislature. Key uncertainty.
6. Legal challenges — e.g., the Democracy Docket court ruling on the title/summary.
7. California is 80%+ vote-by-mail (VBM). Adding a 4-digit requirement to the envelope = risk of ballot rejection if a single digit is wrong. Are there cure procedures? The Mercury News interview says "assuming eligible voters receive notice and the opportunity to correct errors" — but what does the actual measure say? Let me check the text of the measure for details on rejected ballots and provisional ballots.

Also, the key question is "is it better to vote yes or no?" — I need to make a judgment. Let me think through the arguments:

Arguments in favor of YES:
- Low-cost voter fraud is essentially nonexistent, but ID requirements increase trust in elections (public trust is a real problem post-2020).
- Most Americans support voter ID (polls show majority support; in California, the LA Times editorial? Let me check the editorial).
- Free voter ID cards for those who don't have one.
- The measure includes good governance elements: citizenship verification, audits, clean-up of the voter rolls.
- Bipartisan support among the general public (not politicians).

Arguments in favor of NO:
- Empirical research shows that strict voter ID laws have little to no effect on preventing fraud (fraud is rare), but they can suppress turnout, particularly among minorities, the elderly, low-income voters, and people of color. The Texas 2013 study (Franklin et al., University of Chicago / the Brennan Center?) — actually the famous study is "Voter ID Laws and Turnout" — the 2013 Texas law study by Mitchell Franklin et al. found that the 2013 Texas photo ID law reduced Black turnout by about 6 percentage points in 2014.
- In California, over 80% of voters vote by mail. Requiring 4 digits to be written on the envelope creates a new rejection/error pathway. One digit wrong → ballot invalidated. This is an "accuracy" risk that could be significant in a VBM state. California already does signature verification + cure.
- Cost: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year.
- Privacy/security concerns about writing SSN digits on the envelope.
- The measure is vague: which IDs qualify is up to the legislature — this is a significant weakness; it could lead to litigation and inconsistent implementation across counties.
- Non-citizen voting is a tiny problem (estimated at a small fraction of a percent of votes), and the existing process already requires citizenship certification under penalty of perjury.
- The ACLU, LWVCA, and Common Cause are opposed; Senator Padilla is also opposing; Newsom and Pelosi are also opposing.
- The "best efforts" citizenship verification could lead to erroneous purges of citizens (a real documented problem: states purging people through data matching mistakes, e.g., the 2011 Harvard study on purges in North Carolina, Florida).

Additional considerations: the measure's title is "Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present a government-issued ID" — note that it's a constitutional amendment, which is hard to change later. And it says "prohibits citizens from voting" — actually, the title is somewhat dramatic.

Key nuance from the analysis: "Implementation of Proposition 39 requires legislative action. The legislature must pass additional laws to implement this measure. The legislature must clarify several details not defined in the measure, such as which forms of ID can be used and which procedures count as 'best efforts' to verify the citizenship status of registered voters."

This is a big deal: the measure's core mechanisms depend on future legislation, so there's a risk of uncertainty/fragmentation.

Also, a Mercury News interview with the No-on-Prop 39 campaign: "When Texas tried this, they threw out 12 times as many mail-in ballots as California."

Let me research:
1. Franklin's study on the impact of the Texas 2013 voter ID law on turnout.
2. Data on the scale of non-citizen voting.
3. California's 2024 rejected ballot figures.
4. What the text of the measure says about rejected/provisional ballots (is there a cure procedure?).
5. Opinions of the editorial boards (e.g., NYT, WSJ, LA Times editorials on Prop 39).
6. Which IDs qualify per the measure or the proponents.

Let me run the searches in parallel.

approximately $190 billion.

stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several

significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to

year from 2028–29 onward.

funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.

The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.
(d) The loss of billions in federal funding further
stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to
reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source
of health coverage for half of all births statewide.
Recent years have seen closures of vital maternity
wards and emergency departments, all attributed in

2. (b) Each time a voter casts a ballot in person, they must present government-issued identification. If voting by mail, they must provide the last 4 digits of a unique identification number from government-issued identification that matches what was specified at registration. "Government-issued identification means a document that permits conclusive verification of the voter's identity." The state shall, upon request, provide a free voter ID card to any eligible voter.
3. (c) This section is self-executing. The legislature shall "promptly enact legislation to implement this section, provide for voting by military and overseas voters in a manner consistent with federal law, and ensure that all state and local officials comply with and support compliance with this section." This is very interesting. The text of Proposition 39 (the main section of the amendment) is short and extremely vague. The full text of the amendment is only a few clauses (Section 3.1 of Article II):

1. (a) Elections officials shall maintain accurate voter rolls, "use best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data," and report annually the percentage of voter rolls in each county whose citizenship has been verified.
2. (b) Each time a voter casts a ballot in person, they must present government-issued identification. If voting by mail, they must provide the last 4 digits of a unique identification number from government-issued identification that matches what was specified at registration. The type of ID specified must be recorded in the voter registration record, noted on the mail ballot envelope, and available via phone or electronically upon request. Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting and confirming that the person cast only one ballot. "Government-issued identification means a document that permits conclusive verification of the voter's identity." The state shall, upon request, provide a free voter ID card to any eligible voter.
3. (c) This section is self-executing. The legislature shall "promptly enact legislation to implement this section, provide for voting by military and overseas voters in a manner consistent with federal law, and ensure that all state and local officials comply with and support compliance with this section." Citizens may seek judicial review. The State Auditor shall audit compliance in odd-numbered years.

Major observations:

1. No mention of a cure/correction procedure for a mismatched 4-digit ID on the mail ballot envelope. The current signature mismatch process has an explicit cure process. The text does not specify what happens if a voter enters the wrong 4 digits on the envelope — the ballot appears to simply not be counted. There is no cure right in the text. The Mercury News interview suggested that the No campaign's position is "assuming eligible voters receive notice and the opportunity to correct errors" — meaning such a mechanism is not explicitly provided for in the text.

2. No definition of which forms of ID qualify ("a document that permits conclusive verification of the voter's identity" — vague), no list. The Legislature is expected to "promptly enact legislation," but this amendment is a constitutional amendment and is self-executing, and the legislature can restrict voting rights... In fact, the legislature has the power to define the details, but the constitutional mandate that in-person voting requires ID is immediately in force, and counties must implement it. There is a risk of inconsistency across counties (58 counties).

3. Note that the ballot measure text says "citizenship verification using government data" — this could lead to erroneous purges (removal of citizens). "Best efforts" is undefined.

4. The claim about non-citizen voting: a 2026 Census Bureau report (which appears to have been published during the Trump administration) claims more than 24,000 non-citizen votes in the 2020 election out of about 128 million (0.019%), but experts criticize the methodology as flawed (possibility of false positives due to data matching). Even taking the report at face value, it's extremely small and would not change election outcomes. Prior studies (Brennan Center, Harvard) found non-citizen voting to be extremely rare. In other words, the problem the measure targets (non-citizen voting, voter fraud) is very small, while the costs (costs, administrative burden, risk of rejecting legitimate ballots) are substantial.

Total rejections 971,007? Hmm, this table is hard to parse. Let me look for the statewide total for 2024. I recall the No campaign claimed that more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches in the November 2024 election. Actually, I think the figure cited in the pro argument was "in the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches, and more than 200,000 voters were troubled." Hmm, wait — I think that was about the signature mismatch count. Let me check the SOS statewide summary. The PDF I found is county-by-county. Let me look for the statewide total.

Also, the No-on-Prop. 39 rebuttal claims: "When Texas tried this, 12 times as many mail ballots were rejected as in California." Let me verify: 2022 Texas mail ballot rejection rate — in Texas in 2022, about 2.3% of mail ballots were rejected? Actually, in the November 2022 Texas election, about 367,000 mail ballots were rejected, and 9.4% of mail ballots were... hmm, let me search. Actually, the claim "12 times" may be comparing Texas's rejection rate. Let me verify quickly.

Also, I should check: does this measure's mail ballot requirement replace or add to the signature? It says "provide the last 4 digits" — signature verification probably continues (since it's not repealed). So voters will have both the signature and the 4 digits. Both failure modes.

More importantly: the measure says a voter must "specify" an ID at registration for mail voting. If an existing voter doesn't specify one by some deadline, they may not be able to vote by mail. According to the Legislative Analyst (LAO), "new and existing voters must specify a government-issued ID at voter registration in order to vote by mail." The Legislature must specify the details. This could lead to large-scale voter confusion.

At this point, I've gathered a lot of information. Main findings:

**Funding**: This measure was drafted by Republican state assemblymember Carl DeMaio (Reform California). It's funded by out-of-state Republican billionaires: Richard Uihlein ($17 million), Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia (currently a White House official) ($8 million), Steven Bray ($3 million in loans + donations), the Winklevoss twins, Nicole Shanahan, Julie Luckey's "Californians for Voter ID" committee (Luckey's mother), and others. Yes total is about $28–36 million, No total is about $3.7–11 million.

**Polling**: A recent Berkeley IGS poll: "When voters were given the additional context that supporters say this measure is necessary to prevent fraud and opponents say it could disenfranchise eligible voters, [support dropped]" (cut off mid-sentence, but the implication is that support declined). Another poll (per an AP article in the Hastings Tribune): nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose, over a third support; more than half of voters with no party preference oppose. Skelton: "The measure is expected to be headed for defeat, largely because Democratic voters in this deep-blue state are conflating it with a discredited president."

**Editorials**: The overwhelming majority of California editorial boards recommend NO: SF Chronicle, McClatchy California (Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee, San Luis Obispo Tribune), San Diego Union-Tribune, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Daily Cal (Berkeley), LA Times (Skelton column + voter guide "clearly no"), etc. Some YES: LA Daily News editorial board (October 15, 2026), Press-Enterprise (Riverside) editorial board "Yes on Proposition 39." A bill Jones guest op-ed in the LA Times argues in favor.

**Empirical evidence**:
- Noncitizen voting is extremely rare: even a disputed Census Bureau report claims 24,000 out of 128 million (0.019%) with a flawed methodology; past studies find it to be negligible; the Brennan Center interviewed 42 jurisdictions; no instance of it affecting an election outcome.
- Voter fraud/impersonation is vanishingly rare (documented cases are at most a handful per election cycle).
- The impact of strict voter ID laws on turnout is mixed, but multiple studies (Hajnal et al., the UCSD/MIT Election Lab's "Disproportionate Burden," Kuk et al. 2020) find that strict ID laws increase the racial gap and depress minority turnout, particularly in primaries. GAO: 4 of 10 studies found a decline of 1.5–3.9 points. A strong NBER study (Mycoff? no—the "difference-in-differences design" one) found no significant effect. The evidence is mixed overall, but when effects are detected, they fall on minorities / low-SES voters.
- Directly relevant case study: Texas SB1 required the last 4 digits of a driver's license / SSN to match the registration on the mail-in ballot envelope → 12.4% of mail-in ballots were rejected in the March 2022 primary (a 12-fold increase from about 1%). Most rejections were due to ID mismatches. This is precisely the mechanism of Prop 39 for the roughly 80% of California voters who vote by mail. In the 2022 Texas general election, the rejection rate was 2.7% (still higher than typical).
- California's current system already requires the DL/state ID/last 4 digits of SSN at registration (which serves as an ID check), and there's signature matching + cure process for mail-in ballots; in-person voters sign a roll.
- Prop 39's text has no cure mechanism for a mismatched 4-digit number on the envelope. (The No campaign's framing in Mercury News suggests there is no cure procedure.)
- Cost: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions annually (LAO).
- The measure is vague: what counts as a qualifying ID is up to the legislature; "best efforts" at citizenship verification is undefined — this risks erroneous purges and litigation; it also includes a citizen's right to sue over compliance (SF Chronicle: "a never-ending lawsuit," "creating a CEQA of voting rights").
- California is about 80% VBM, and adding a second, error-prone identity check on top of signature matching adds friction and a new rejection pathway; the count is already slow (AB 3184 already extends certification up to E+28).
- The measure's supporters claim that over 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatches in the most recent election — per the SOS data, in the 2024 general, "non-matching signature" rejections per county: Alameda 3,092; Contra Costa 2,666; Fresno 2,462; etc. Statewide is probably around 30–40k for non-matching signatures, plus 20–30k for "no voter signature" (I'd need to sum the statewide total, but the "over 100,000" figure might be the total rejections including "contact county" or suspense ballots). Either way, cure is available for signature issues, and the rejection rate is around 1% or less.

Another consideration: does Prop 39 replace signature matching or add to it? The measure doesn't repeal signature verification; it says the official "shall count the ballot only after verifying the voter's identity... and verifying that the person cast only one ballot." So both requirements probably coexist → double friction.

Another angle: is there evidence that ID requirements reduce fraud in a way that justifies the cost? Fraud (impersonation) is extremely rare; the main measurable effect is administrative. Also, a free state-issued voter ID card is a genuinely good element, but it requires the legislature to create a whole new ID infrastructure (like a driver's license) — a big bureaucratic task, which is why the cost is in the tens-to-hundreds of millions annually.

Additionally, this measure is a constitutional amendment — it's difficult to repeal later (requires a 2/3 legislative vote + voter approval, or another initiative). The SF Chronicle's "CEQA of voting rights" point: it creates a standing for private lawsuits, with citizens being able to seek judicial review over any county's compliance.

The question asks: "On this measure, is it better to vote yes or no? … Answer with only `yes` or `no`."

Given the weight of the research:
- The problem this measure is trying to solve (noncitizen voting / voter fraud) is vanishingly small and not empirically demonstrated at any meaningful scale.
- The mechanism (last 4 digits on the mail-in envelope) has direct precedent in Texas, where it caused a 12-fold spike in mail-in ballot rejections.
- California is 80%+ mail-in voting; there is no cure mechanism in the text; a single wrong digit = rejected ballot.
- Costs are high (tens to low hundreds of millions annually).
- The measure is vague, likely to generate litigation, and could produce inconsistent implementation across 58 counties.
- "Best efforts" at citizenship verification could lead to erroneous purges of citizens.
- Research on strict ID laws shows, when effects are found, that they disproportionately burden voters of color, the poor, the elderly, and rural voters.
- Nearly all of California's major newspapers and editorial boards, voting rights organizations, and the state's political establishment recommend No.
- Polls show declining / a majority opposition among likely voters.

The arguments for Yes (trust, bipartisan support, free ID) are about perception; the measure does preserve mail voting and extended hours, but those are also preserved under a No vote. The core "integrity" benefits are largely duplicative of existing checks (the ID at registration, signature matching, perjury penalties).

Weighing everything, the better vote based on this research is NO.

Answer: no

I have now completed extensive research. Here's a synthesis of my findings before giving my answer:

**What Prop. 39 does (2026 California election):**
- Requires a government ID to vote in person every time
- Requires the last four digits of a designated government ID number on mail ballot envelopes, which must exactly match the registration record — mismatch means the ballot is not counted, and **the text contains no cure mechanism** for a wrong digit (unlike the current signature-mismatch process, which has an explicit cure window)
- Requires "best efforts" citizenship verification using government data, with annual county reporting
- Creates a free state voter ID card; costs "tens of millions to low hundreds of millions" per year (nonpartisan Legislative Analyst)
- Is vague — which IDs qualify is left to the Legislature; includes a private right of litigation over compliance

**Key evidence:**
- **The problem it solves is vanishingly small:** Noncitizen voting estimates top out at ~24,000 of 128M votes (0.019%) in a disputed Census report with flawed methodology; voter impersonation fraud is documented at only a handful of cases per cycle.
- **Direct precedent for its core mechanism:** Texas's near-identical "last four digits on the envelope" requirement caused mail ballot rejections to spike **12× to ~12.4%** in the 2022 primary — 1 in 8 mailed ballots thrown out, mostly over ID mismatches. California is ~80% mail-voting.
- **Research on strict ID laws** is mixed but, where effects are found (UCSD/UC Berkeley, MIT Election Lab, GAO), they fall disproportionately on voters of color, low-income, elderly, and rural voters — not on fraud prevention.
- **California already verifies identity**: at registration (DL/ID/SSN last four) and via signature matching with cure procedures for mail ballots.
- **Who's behind it:** Assemblyman Carl DeMaio (Reform California), funded largely by out-of-state billionaires (Richard Uihlein $17M, Joe Gebbia $8M, Steven Bray, Winklevoss, Shanahan); opposed by ACLU, LWVCA, Common Cause, and the state's establishment (Padilla, Newsom, Pelosi).
- **Editorial consensus in California:** SF Chronicle, McClatchy (Sacramento Bee et al.), San Diego Union-Tribune, Santa Cruz Sentinel, LA Times ("flat no"), and others all recommend NO; a few (Press-Enterprise, LA Daily News) say Yes.
- **Polling:** ~6 in 10 likely voters oppose; support "dwindled" once voters heard details; even among independents/no-party, more than half oppose.

The measure adds a new, error-prone rejection pathway to an already-secure, largely mail-based system, at high cost, to fix a fraud problem that research consistently finds to be negligible, while introducing litigation risk and vagueness into a constitutional amendment.

**no**

I have now completed extensive research. Here's a synthesis of my findings before giving my answer:

**What Prop. 39 does (2026 California election):**
- Requires a government ID to vote in person every time
- Requires the last four digits of a designated government ID number on mail ballot envelopes, which must exactly match the registration record — mismatch means the ballot is not counted, and **the text contains no cure mechanism** for a wrong digit (unlike the current signature-mismatch process, which has an explicit cure window)
- Requires "best efforts" citizenship verification using government data, with annual county reporting
- Creates a free state voter ID card; costs "tens of millions to low hundreds of millions" per year (nonpartisan Legislative Analyst)
- Is vague — which IDs qualify is left to the Legislature; includes a private right of litigation over compliance

**Key evidence:**
- **The problem it solves is vanishingly small:** Noncitizen voting estimates top out at ~24,000 of 128M votes (0.019%) in a disputed Census report with flawed methodology; voter impersonation fraud is documented at only a handful of cases per cycle.
- **Direct precedent for its core mechanism:** Texas's near-identical "last four digits on the envelope" requirement caused mail ballot rejections to spike **12× to ~12.4%** in the 2022 primary — 1 in 8 mailed ballots thrown out, mostly over ID mismatches. California is ~80% mail-voting.
- **Research on strict ID laws** is mixed but, where effects are found (UCSD/UC Berkeley, MIT Election Lab, GAO), they fall disproportionately on voters of color, low-income, elderly, and rural voters — not on fraud prevention.
- **California already verifies identity**: at registration (DL/ID/SSN last four) and via signature matching with cure procedures for mail ballots.
- **Who's behind it:** Assemblyman Carl DeMaio (Reform California), funded largely by out-of-state billionaires (Richard Uihlein $17M, Joe Gebbia $8M, Steven Bray, Winklevoss, Shanahan); opposed by ACLU, LWVCA, Common Cause, and the state's establishment (Padilla, Newsom, Pelosi).
- **Editorial consensus in California:** SF Chronicle, McClatchy (Sacramento Bee et al.), San Diego Union-Tribune, Santa Cruz Sentinel, LA Times ("flat no"), and others all recommend NO; a few (Press-Enterprise, LA Daily News) say Yes.
- **Polling:** ~6 in 10 likely voters oppose; support "dwindled" once voters heard details; even among independents/no-party, more than half oppose.

The measure adds a new, error-prone rejection pathway to an already-secure, largely mail-based system, at high cost, to fix a fraud problem that research consistently finds to be negligible, while introducing litigation risk and vagueness into a constitutional amendment.

**no**

39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
CON
No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.
